groups.title: Setting out
groups.explanation: Each account begins with a boat journey. Read the different amounts of scene-setting.

groups.title: The storm and the appeal
groups.explanation: Notice how each account voices the disciples’ appeal.

groups.title: Calm, faith, and wonder
groups.explanation: Luke’s calming of the storm is already in verse 24 above. These are thematic reading groups, not exact sentence alignments.

notes.title: Notice the order
notes.text: In Matthew, Jesus questions the disciples before calming the storm (8:26). In Mark and Luke, the question about faith follows the calming (Mark 4:39–40; Luke 8:24–25). This is an observation about these passages; it does not by itself establish how they were composed.

notes.title: A question about understanding
notes.text: Dale B. Martin reads Mark’s disciples’ question about Jesus in 4:41 within a wider narrative pattern: the disciples struggle to understand him. This is Martin’s literary interpretation, not a claim that this scene independently establishes what the historical disciples knew.

citations.locator: Chapter 2, “A Historical Critical Reading of Mark” (begins 13:44); transcript discussion of Mark 4:41

notes.title: From comparison to interpretation
notes.text: Martin describes redaction criticism as studying how an author edits source material to communicate a message. That method depends on an argued account of the sources. Here, the alignment helps you notice the texts before choosing a theory about their relationship.

citations.locator: Chapter 5 (begins 35:44), explanation of redaction criticism; the lecture’s example is Matthew 14, a different sea episode

comparisons.title: The Lord’s Prayer
comparisons.subtitle: A shared prayer in two settings

groups.title: How Jesus introduces the prayer
groups.explanation: In Matthew, the prayer follows teaching about how to pray. In Luke, a disciple asks Jesus to teach the group to pray.

groups.title: The address and opening requests
groups.explanation: Both prayers address God as Father and ask for his name to be honored and his kingdom to come. Matthew also asks for God’s will to be done on earth as in heaven.

groups.title: Bread for the day
groups.explanation: Compare the timing of the request for bread. Matthew says “today” and Luke says “each day.”

groups.title: Forgiveness and temptation
groups.explanation: Both versions connect receiving forgiveness with forgiving others. Matthew closes with an additional request for deliverance from the evil one.

notes.title: Two settings for a shared prayer
notes.text: Matthew gives the prayer during the Sermon on the Mount. Luke introduces it with a disciple’s request after Jesus finishes praying. Read the verses before the prayer and notice how each Gospel gives the teaching a different introduction.

notes.title: How might the prayer have reached both Gospels?
notes.text: Mark Goodacre uses the Lord’s Prayer as an example of material shared by Matthew and Luke outside Mark. A common written source (Q) and Luke’s use of Matthew offer two possible explanations for that broader pattern. Olegs Andrejevs also examines a proposal that the prayer circulated in worship apart from Q. The two versions give us a place to test these explanations alongside other parallels.
